worker_scope: 04 SOURCE EXECUTOR — Aegean (round-6 worker supplement-opencode-1, assignment 04)

audits.question: Verify the entry's distinction between undeciphered Linear A/Minoan affiliation and readable Greek Linear B: sign similarity and B-based transliteration are not proof of Minoan pronunciation, meaning or divine names.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/aegean-minoan-mycenaean.md §3 table rows 'Language affiliation', 'Reading status', 'Script relationship', 'Unsafe inference' (lines 51-56); line 63 'applying a Linear B value to a similar Linear A sign is not proof of its exact Minoan pronunciation, much less the word's meaning'; line 103 (Minoan divine names not securely readable; da-ma-te = Déméter a contested proposal, not a decipherment, per Salgarella 2022); §11 line 198 (unsettled questions)
audits.entry_claim: Linear A remains undeciphered as a language and its underlying language or languages are not securely assigned to any family; although it shares many signs with Linear B, conventional B-based transliterations are only analytical notation, so applying a Linear B value to a similar Linear A sign proves neither Minoan pronunciation nor word meaning nor divine names (the da-ma-te = Déméter proposal is a contested etymological argument, not a decipherment), whereas Linear B is deciphered Mycenaean Greek whose accounts reveal names, offices, and cult recipients.
audits.source_citation: Rutter, Jeremy B. (n.d.), Aegean Prehistoric Archaeology, Dartmouth College open teaching text, Lesson 15 'Minoan Religion', section 'The Nature of the Evidence' (one of the entry's own cited sources).
audits.source_locator: Lesson 15, opening section 'The Nature of the Evidence', first paragraph (unpaginated web page as served 2026-10-17)
audits.source_excerpt: Since Linear A is as yet undeciphered, there is effectively no contemporary textual evidence regarding Minoan religion.
audits.retrieval_method: public HTTP(S) fetch (FetchURL tool) of the entry-cited open Dartmouth teaching page; full page text inspected in-session; same paragraph continues that even a future decipherment would yield little beyond the names of divinities
audits.basis: The retrieved passage directly confirms the Linear A half of the entry's contrast: the script is undeciphered, so there is no readable Minoan religious or divine-name content today, and the same paragraph warns even a decipherment would likely give little beyond divine names - so B-based values on similar Linear A signs cannot yield Minoan pronunciation, meaning, or divine names. The Linear B half is confirmed by two corroboration passages retrieved this round: LiBER (CNR) documents Ventris's decipherment of Linear B as Greek via the Kober/Bennett sign-frequency work, and Rutter's lesson 26 prints transliterated Greek divine-name lists from the Knossos and Pylos tablets while stating that no Linear B figure can be convincingly connected with the dove or snake goddesses of Minoan art. Both poles of the entry's bounded distinction - undeciphered Minoan side, readable Greek side - are thus backed by actual retrieved text.
audits.coupling_implication: Coupled entries (writing-systems, historical-linguistics, naming-systems, pantheon-archetypes) must keep script, language, and religion layers separate: transliterated Linear A sign groups may be used only as analytical notation; no fictional Minoan divine name, pronunciation, or meaning may be presented as recovered; readable Greek Linear B names are usable anchors precisely because Linear B is deciphered.
audits.limits: Salgarella 2022 (Oxford Classical Dictionary / Oxford Research Encyclopedia), the entry's named warrant for 'not securely assigned to any family' and 'untenable identifications', returned HTTP 403 (bot wall) on 2026-10-17 and was not ground against it - the unaffiliation wording is therefore tested only indirectly (undeciphered status plus absence of readable Minoan text), not by her own sentences. Duhoux 1997 (Minos 29-30, da-ma-te = Déméter?) was located only as bibliographic metadata on Dialnet; its item-level argument was not retrieved. A 2026 popular-press item on a new Linear A Demeter/Dionysos proposal was discarded: the arXiv ID cited in coverage resolved to an unrelated robotics paper, so the thread stayed unverifiable. Dartmouth teaching pages are dated in places (the entry itself flags this); timestamps in this fragment are minute-approximate from the session log. Round tooling note: WebSearch quota failed mid-round (HTTP 403 usage limit); retrieval used DuckDuckGo HTML result pages plus direct URL fetches. Language/edition/mediator statement: every quoted passage was inspected in English (Rutter teaching text; LiBER and BMCR pages; English anthology chapters rendering transliterated Mycenaean Greek sign groups with Greek-script glosses); no untranslated non-English primary text was relied on and no worker-made translation substitutes for a published one. All round-6 retrieval notes for this assignment (access failures, refused pirated Killen 2024 scan, scratch inventory) are also mirrored in reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-04/notes.md.

audits.question: Check the relationship and limits between Linear B textile accounts and elite painted/figurine costume: does an actual cited tablet/object/scholarly passage support the claimed material or institutional link without a one-to-one garment identification?
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/aegean-minoan-mycenaean.md §4 table row 'Sheep, wool, textile, and personnel accounts' (line 74); §7 opening line 125 and table rows 'Fresco depictions of dress' (line 131), 'Figurines and modeled costume' (line 132), 'Linear B textile accounts' (line 133, 'cannot establish a secure one-to-one matching of every recorded cloth term to a painted outfit'); §11 'Deliberate gap' line 199
audits.entry_claim: Linear B sheep, wool, textile, and personnel accounts evidence substantial administrative involvement in textile production but record only selected economic categories of wool, cloth, labor, and allocation; together with fresco and figurine imagery (a different evidence class) they cannot establish a secure one-to-one matching of every recorded cloth term to a painted or modeled outfit; the archive records institutional couplings (including cult-side cloth) only at the level of obligations and designations, and no excavated octopus-patterned textile is claimed.
audits.source_citation: Boloti, Tina (2014), 'e-ri-ta's Dress: Contribution to the Study of the Mycenaean Priestesses' Attire', ch. 11 in Harlow, Michel & Nosch (eds), Prehistoric, Ancient Near Eastern and Aegean Textiles and Dress: an interdisciplinary anthology, Ancient Textiles Series 18, Oxbow, pp. 245 ff.; open-access author proof hosted in the University of Copenhagen Curis repository.
audits.source_locator: Chapter 11, p. 246 (printed pagination; PDF page 259 of the Curis portalfiles/183157075 proof file), paragraph beginning 'Although Linear B tablets provide adequate evidence for certain types of dress...'
audits.source_excerpt: Although Linear B tablets provide adequate evidence for certain types of dress (we-a2-no, ki-to, pa-we-a etc.), raw materials and techniques... they offer virtually no direct information as far as priestly attire is concerned.
audits.retrieval_method: public repository download (curl) of the open-access author-proof PDF from the University of Copenhagen Curis repository into the worker's git-ignored scratch subtree (reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-04/); text extracted locally with pdftotext and inspected; no restricted or pirated copy used
audits.basis: The retrieved Boloti sentence, with the next sentence of the same paragraph ('Any attempt to correlate garments recorded in the tablets with those known from the contemporary iconography remains hypothetical or dubious.'), verifies both halves of the entry's bounded claim: the tablets do record garment terms and raw materials as economic data (adequate evidence of the administrative layer), yet they give virtually no direct information about actual elite/ritual attire, and matching recorded cloth terms to painted or modeled outfits stays hypothetical or dubious - exactly the entry's stated limit at line 133 and line 74. Corroborating retrieved passages add the institutional-link side with its hedges (Rutter lesson 26: amphipoloi 'servants of Potnia charged with the care of ceremonial costumes'; anointed oil 'almost certainly not for statues... but perhaps for textiles belonging to deities') and concrete tablet identifiers showing which cloth terms the archive records (Gasbarra: ki-to at KN Lc 563.B and L 693.1, forms at L 771.2, Ld 785.2b, Ld 787.B; Konstantinidi-Syvridi: pa-wo and e-ra-pe-me-na 'sewn' at KN L 647), so an actual cited tablet/scholarly basis exists without any one-to-one garment identification.
audits.coupling_implication: The entry's flock-assessment -> wool-allocation -> patterned-cloth-commission -> official-issue -> festival-display chain can be modeled as an institutional layer, and fresco/figurine costume as a separate display layer, without asserting that recorded cloth terms (pa-we-a2, ki-to, we-a2-no, pa-wo) match any painted outfit; cult-side costume couplings (amphipoloi, anointing-oil-for-textiles) carry explicit scholarly hedging and must stay design proposals, not recovered identifications.
audits.limits: The Boloti/Konstantinidi-Syvridi/Gasbarra chapters are from 2014 and predate the entry's Killen 2024 reference work, which was not directly consulted (Cambridge Core paywalled; the entry's own route - Judson's open BMCR 2024 review - was used instead for its status). A ResearchGate copy of a study on the Knossos Lc(1) textile targets returned HTTP 403 and remained unverified. An archive.org scan of Killen 2024 appeared in search results but was deliberately not used because it is a pirated restricted work. Rutter pages are dated teaching aids (entry flags this). The entry makes no specific-tablet claim, so no tablet number was tested against a fresh epigraphic edition; LiBER's per-document pages sit behind a JavaScript search interface and were not individually retrieved. Excerpt ellipses replace Greek-script glosses; word counts respect the 40-word cap. Language/edition/mediator statement: all quoted passages were read in published English (Oxbow anthology author-proof chapters; Dartmouth teaching text), with Mycenaean cloth terms in standard B-based transliteration; no worker-made translation stands in for a published one. Full retrieval notes (access failures, refused pirated scan, scratch inventory) mirrored in reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-04/notes.md.

corroboration.source_citation: Konstantinidi-Syvridi, Eleni (2014), 'Buttons, Pins, Clips and Belts... "Inconspicuous" Dress Accessories from the Burial Context of the Mycenaean Period (16th-12th cent. BC)', ch. 6 in the same anthology (Ancient Textiles Series 18).

corroboration.source_excerpt: pictorial evidence from the Aegean seems to be restricted to representations of the formal or ritual costume; Linear B tablets document some types of costumes... the short skirt... 'flounced' and a short textile with sleeves (pa-wo)
